steps: A local event increments the Lamport counter.
A sent message carries the current counter.
A node identifier breaks equal timestamps when deterministic total order is needed.

lesson.scenario: Two order workers timestamp local and message events without synchronized wall clocks.

steps.title: Independent counters
steps.narration: A is at 5 and B is at 7 after unrelated local work.
steps.outcome: The counters need not match physical time.
steps.invariant: Each process increments its counter before every event.

steps.title: Send event
steps.narration: A increments to 6 and stamps a reservation message.
steps.outcome: The message carries A logical time 6.
steps.invariant: A send timestamp is greater than A preceding events.

steps.title: Receive merge
steps.narration: B receives stamp 6 and advances to max(7,6)+1=8.
steps.outcome: The receive event is ordered after the send.
steps.invariant: If event x happens before y, Lamport(x) is less than Lamport(y).

steps.title: Reply event
steps.narration: B increments to 9 before sending confirmation.
steps.outcome: The causal chain has increasing timestamps 6, 8, 9.
steps.invariant: Equal counters require a deterministic node-id tie-breaker for total sorting.

steps.title: A merges reply
steps.narration: A receives stamp 9 and advances from 6 to 10.
steps.outcome: The ledger can produce a total order consistent with causality.
steps.invariant: Lamport clocks cannot prove that two differently stamped events were concurrent.

production.scenario: An ecommerce order timeline service uses Lamport clocks to merge payment, fraud, and warehouse events into one stable customer-facing history even when workers publish from skewed machines.
components: Emits card-authorization events for checkout orders
Approves or holds the same order independently of payment
Owns the activity feed shown for each order
Assigns the next logical sequence number per order aggregate
Carries stamped order events to all timeline projectors
Authoritative ordered history for each order
Reads the reconstructed order timeline during escalations
Rebuilds one order timeline after a projector failover
flows: The payment worker reports card approval before the warehouse has published any shipping milestones.
Fraud can independently clear the same order from another machine with a completely different wall clock.
The timeline service increments the logical clock for order 8472 instead of trusting the producer timestamps.
Every downstream consumer now sees the same logical position for that order activity.
The timeline store inserts payment and fraud updates by logical stamp and uses producer ID only to break ties deterministically.
When support opens the order, the feed is identical no matter which worker published first in real time.
After a failover, the replay projector reconstructs the same sequence because Lamport stamps survive consumer restarts.
